questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $2{x}^{4}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14122526/assets/b23ef6e4df05874a715271c578dfa57d5ddacabef2d0801edc4e736c7de66e17.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2{x}^{4}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2{x}^{4}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{4}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2{x}^{4}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14122526/assets/983beaf02582c5ebaee129e28bba657eb2db5e4da7f74eb4b8eba73b9083a259.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x+1.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x+1.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x+1)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}+x+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={1}^{2}+1+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+x+6 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+x+6) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{2({x}^{2}+x+6)}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x>0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is ${2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,{m/s}^{2}$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$ If $P$ has a displacement of $1\,m$ when its velocity is $4\,m/s,$ find $v$ in terms of $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14122526/assets/6ddbfef68a0b41a6ee3f11c46ff7821f7ff0dc23a16b4244b5e7a1f6579d7dd2.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude ${2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-{2}^{2-x}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={2}^{2-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $x=1\,\text{m}$ when $v=4\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2-1}+C \\ 8 & =2+C \\ C & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={2}^{2-x}+6 \\ {v}^{2} & ={2}^{3-x}+12 \\ {v}^{2} & =4({2}^{1-x}+3) \\ v & =\pm 2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2\sqrt{{2}^{1-x}+3}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=1\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14122526/assets/141c6dd6c91841238298b86fac1063c76faeb7cd103e13d2723f6ac05ed58f50.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{32}{(x+2)^{5}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=1\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =\frac{8}{(0+2)^{4}}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{8}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{16}{(x+2)^{4}} \\ v & =\pm \frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{(x+2)^{2}} \\ (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int (x+2)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \frac{1}{3}(x+2)^{3} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ (x+2)^{3} & =12t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=8,$ and the particular solution is

$$
(x+2)^{3}=12t+8.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^{3} & =12t+8 \\ x+2 & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{12t+8}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at $x=1\,m$ and has velocity $v=4\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14122526/assets/f08c9d1e8dce3c0ae7c37719cadc3fc60bf5de3030ce8c44ca7528a98f3abf7e.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $8{e}^{1-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-8{e}^{1-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -8{e}^{1-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =8{e}^{0}+K \\ 8 & =8+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =8{e}^{1-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =16{e}^{1-x} \\ v & =\pm 4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{e}^{(1-x)/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4{e}^{(1-x)/2} \\ \frac{1}{{e}^{(1-x)/2}}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =4 \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{(x-1)/2}\text{d}x & =\int 4\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =4t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=1$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{(x-1)/2}=2t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{(x-1)/2} & =2t+1 \\ \frac{x-1}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x-1 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1)+1.\end{aligned}
$$
